name: Croydon facelift

lead: The Croydon facelift is a British slang name for a hairstyle in which the hair is pulled tightly back from the forehead into a high ponytail or bun. The tension draws the skin upward, which people say lifts the brows and cheeks and smooths lines, like a surgical facelift but without surgery.

The effect lasts only while the hair is tied. The phrase is often used jokingly or derogatorily, linking the look to working-class or 'chav' stereotypes, and appears in the 2008 Chambers Slang Dictionary according to reference sources.

paras: The hair is combed or gelled smooth from the hairline and fastened high on the head with an elastic or pins, typically on straight or straightened hair. It needs little time or product, and the lift is visible immediately.
Wikipedia notes that tight styles of this kind can lead to traction alopecia, a gradual hair loss.

Brows and eyes look lifted and lines look smoother
angle.text: Pulling the hair back tightly creates an immediate, temporary lifting effect on the upper face, which wearers use as a no-cost alternative to a cosmetic procedure. The lift disappears when the hair is released.

lead: The Croydon facelift is English slang for a hairstyle in which the hair is pulled tightly back and tied in a high ponytail or bun. It is believed to lift the skin of the forehead and face, imitating a facelift.[1]

Its appearance payoff is immediate: the pull raises the brows and corners of the eyes, tautens the forehead and cheeks, and temporarily smooths fine lines, which can emphasise cheekbones and eye shape.[2] It requires only a comb, elastic or pins and some styling product.[2]

The term is considered derogatory because it ties the hairstyle to Croydon and to lower-class stereotypes, though Wikipedia notes any unfashionable area could replace Croydon in the phrase; regional variants include 'council house facelift' and 'Millie facelift' in Northern Ireland.[1] Wikipedia also records the Croydon Guardian joking that the style might date back to Nefertiti.[1]
infobox: Council house facelift, Essex facelift, Millie facelift

paras: The style scrapes the hair back from the forehead and temples, usually into a high ponytail or bun, so that the tension elevates the brows and stretches the facial skin.[1][2] It is typically done on straight or straightened hair, using gel, pins or strong-hold bands.[2]

Wikipedia says no verified first use is known.[1] Grokipedia reports a Croydon Guardian reference dated 13 August 2003, and says the 2008 Chambers Slang Dictionary defined the term as a hairstyle that pulls the hair tightly back to give the effect of a facelift.[2] Tight pulled-back ponytails and buns appear throughout history, from Minoan art to Victorian work styles, though those earlier styles were not described as lift effects.[2]

Media have portrayed the look as typical of young working-class women and the 'chav' subculture, and the term is regarded as derogatory.[1][2] Some wearers treat it simply as a quick grooming shortcut that gives an immediate boost.[2]
Sustained tight hairstyles can cause traction alopecia, a gradual loss of hair at the hairline.[1]

timeline.event: A Croydon Guardian article of 13 August is reported as an early media reference to the term.[2]
Chambers Slang Dictionary records the phrase.[2]
